sections.title: The Gothic
sections.description: Part of the reason the Gothic remains compelling lies in its opaque origins and opportunistic nature. It's a term we use for speaking about a body of writing anchored in multiple literary traditions, uncannily present whether we are speaking of power, desire, identity, or the numinous. Less a genre than an aesthetic that crosses them -- or both at once -- it seems to move effortlessly, almost virally, across media, ideologies, and national traditions. This seminar, therefore, will double as a seminar on genre, and will consider post-structural, affective, queer, and sociological approaches to Gothic's identities, histories, and tendencies. We'll ask less what Gothic is that than where it has resided (and resides) and what it has signified (and can signify). We’ll take a two-step approach. For the first 8-10 weeks of the seminar, we’ll move through key texts from gothic's first meteoric rise, 1760-1830. Possible authors include Jane Austen, Joanna Ballie, Charles Brockden Brown, Edmund Burke, Lord Byron, Samuel Coleridge, George Colman the Younger, Olaudah Equiano, James Hogg, John Keats, Matthew Lewis, Edgar Allan Poe, Ann Radcliffe, Mary Robinson, Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley, Percy Shelley, Mary Wollstonecraft, and William Wordsworth, which we’ll read these alongside short works by Jacques Derrida, Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, Jack Halberstam, Anna Barbauld, the Marquis de Sade, Sigmund Freud, and others. Depending on the size and interests of the seminar, we may then move beyond these historical confines to other periods, media, and national traditions, from Saxon spells, medieval mysteries, and early modern revenge tragedies to Victorian sensation fiction, fin-de-siecle decadence, early silent film, Hollywood Cinema, and more recent works of fiction (Piranesi, Zone One, Mexican Gothic, Lovecraft Country), film (Alien, Ringu, Thirst, Get Out, Tumbbad, Us, His House), and TV (Penny Dreadful, Dead Loch, How to Get to Heaven from Belfast). Assignments will include at least one short presentation, a few responses, an annotated bibliography, and a final conference presentation and essay.
